title: Hypoallergenic Carpet: What's Real and What's Marketing
meta: No carpet is truly hypoallergenic. What is real: low dense pile, Green Label Plus, the right pad and humidity control. Wills Flooring, Everett carpet experts.
keywords: hypoallergenic carpet, best carpet for allergies, is hypoallergenic carpet real, low VOC carpet for asthma, carpet installation Everett WA

blocks.lead: "Hypoallergenic carpet" is a marketing term with no legal definition or testing standard behind it. What is real: a short, dense pile that vacuums clean, a synthetic fiber that does not feed dust mites, a Green Label Plus certification for low emissions, and a house kept under 50 percent humidity.
blocks.detail: Wills Flooring brings carpet samples to Everett homes every week, and the allergy question comes up in most of them. This post separates the claims that hold up from the ones printed on the back of the sample board.

blocks.html: Everett is a damp city. Riverside and Bayside houses from the 1910s sit on crawlspaces, Silver Lake and Eastmont homes from the 90s have carpet in every bedroom, and Port Gardner condos hold humidity through a long gray winter. Dust mites, which cause more indoor allergy symptoms than anything else, love exactly that. So when a sample board promises hypoallergenic carpet, the real question is whether the carpet and the way you live with it keep mites, dander and pollen from building up. Some of the marketing points at real features. Some of it is just a word.

head: Claim on the sample board
Real or marketing
What is actually going on
rows: No agency defines or tests it for carpet. It usually means the fiber is synthetic and the pile is short, which are real features you can check yourself.
An independent emissions test run by the Carpet and Rug Institute. It limits VOCs from the carpet, the pad and the adhesive. Look for the logo on the actual product, not the brand.
Slows mold growth on the fiber in a lab. Does nothing about dust mites, dander or pollen, which are the allergens that matter.
Soil-resistant fiber releases dirt to the vacuum more easily, which means fewer trapped particles over time. It is a cleaning benefit that helps allergies.
Keeps spills and pet accidents from soaking into the pad and subfloor, where mold and odor start. Worth it in a damp Everett home.

blocks.text: What actually lowers allergens in a carpeted room

items.title: Short, dense pile
items.text: A low loop or a dense short cut pile has less depth for mites and dander to settle into and lets a vacuum reach the backing. Deep frieze and shag hold more and release less. Density matters more than fiber for this.

items.title: A vacuum with a sealed HEPA system
items.text: The carpet is only as clean as the machine. A sealed HEPA vacuum used twice a week removes what the carpet has caught. A leaky bagless unit blows it back into the air, which is the real source of the "carpet made my allergies worse" stories.

items.title: Humidity under 50 percent
items.text: Dust mites cannot survive below about 50 percent relative humidity. In Everett that means a dehumidifier in winter, bathroom fans that vent outside, and a dry crawlspace under an older Riverside house. No carpet choice replaces this.

items.title: Hot-water extraction once a year
items.text: Professional cleaning pulls out what vacuuming misses and restores soil resistance. Let it dry fully with fans running. Carpet that stays damp for days is a mold problem, not an allergy solution.

blocks.title: The first 72 hours matter more than the label:
blocks.text: New carpet, pad and any seam sealer release most of their odor in the first three days. Open windows, run fans, and keep an asthmatic child or a sensitive adult out of the room until the smell is gone. Green Label Plus lowers this; it does not eliminate it.
When carpet is the wrong answer, whatever the label says

a.title: Choose a low, dense carpet when
items: Symptoms are mild and seasonal, mostly pollen
The room is a bedroom that will be vacuumed twice a week with a sealed HEPA machine
The house holds under 50 percent humidity through winter
You want warmth and quiet in a Port Gardner condo with sound rules

b.title: Skip carpet when
items: A doctor has named dust mites or mold as the trigger
Someone in the house has asthma that sends them to urgent care
The room is a basement or sits over a damp crawlspace
Pets sleep in the room and accidents are likely

blocks.html: For the second column, a hard floor plus a washable area rug gives you the softness without the reservoir. Vinyl plank is the usual pick in Everett bedrooms and basements because it handles moisture; see carpet vs vinyl plank for bedrooms for that comparison. blocks.text: Mistakes that undo an allergy-friendly carpet

items.html: Buying by the word on the label. Two carpets can both say hypoallergenic while one is a dense low loop and the other a tall plush. Turn the sample over, check the pile height and the density, and look for the Green Label Plus mark.
Keeping the old pad. Pad absorbs a decade of dander and spills. Always replace it, and ask for a moisture-barrier pad in rooms with pets or a history of leaks.
Installing over a damp subfloor. A musty smell in an older Everett house is usually the crawlspace, not the carpet. Fix the moisture first or the new carpet becomes the new mold host.
Skipping the vacuum upgrade. A low-pile carpet with a bad vacuum is worse than a plush with a good one. The machine is part of the flooring budget.

Carpeting the whole house to solve a bedroom problem. Put the allergy-friendly carpet where the sensitive person sleeps, and use hard floors in the hallways and living areas that carry the most traffic and dirt.

blocks.text: What to check at the sample stage

items: Pile height under half an inch and a density you can feel by pressing your thumb into the sample.
The Green Label Plus logo on the carpet, the pad and any adhesive the installer plans to use.
Synthetic fiber, ideally nylon or triexta, with soil-release treatment.
A moisture-barrier pad option for pet rooms and any room over a crawlspace.
Tack strip installation rather than glue-down where possible, so there is less adhesive in the room.

faq.q: Is there a carpet that is truly hypoallergenic?
faq.a: No. The term is not defined or tested by any agency for carpet. What you can buy is a low, dense synthetic carpet with Green Label Plus certification, which limits emissions and is easy to vacuum clean. That combination, plus humidity control, is what actually reduces allergy symptoms.

faq.q: Does carpet make allergies worse than hard floors?
faq.a: It depends on the allergen and the cleaning. Carpet holds particles out of the air until it is disturbed, and a sealed HEPA vacuum removes them. For dust-mite and mold allergies, though, a hard floor is easier to keep clean and dry, and most allergists recommend it in the bedroom.

faq.q: What is Green Label Plus and does it matter?
faq.a: It is an independent low-emission certification from the Carpet and Rug Institute for carpet, pad and adhesive. It matters for the first days after installation, when new carpet off-gasses the most. It says nothing about dust mites or dander, so pair it with a low, dense pile.

faq.q: Which fiber is best for someone with allergies?
faq.a: Nylon or triexta in a short, dense construction. Both are synthetic, hold their shape, and release soil to a vacuum. Wool is natural and low in emissions but holds more dust and sheds early. Polyester is fine on a budget but is usually sold in taller piles that trap more.

faq.q: Why does Everett humidity matter for carpet and allergies?
faq.a: Dust mites need humidity above roughly 50 percent to survive. Everett winters keep many homes above that, especially older houses over crawlspaces and condos with poor ventilation. A dehumidifier, vented bath fans and a dry crawlspace do more for mite allergies than any carpet choice.

faq.q: Should I replace the carpet pad if I only replace the carpet?
faq.a: Yes, always. Old pad holds years of dander, dust and spills, and it is the layer you cannot vacuum. New pad with a moisture barrier is the right choice for pet rooms and any room where a spill or accident is likely.
